channel.title: Defer Nothing
channel.description: Defer Nothing is Abir Sarkar's practical book on designing, building, testing, and operating production backend services in Go. Read the introduction, Part I, and Part II free on goholic.in.

item.title: Introduction
item.description: Why this book exists: Go gets you to real backend problems faster, and Defer Nothing is the habit of deciding how a service fails at the moment you decide how it works.
item.author: Abir Sarkar

item.title: Chapter 1: What Is a Backend, Really?
item.description: A backend is a state-transforming system, not a request handler. Chapter 1 maps the seven stages of a request and the eight concerns that follow.
item.author: Abir Sarkar

item.title: Chapter 2: From Request to Response
item.description: A physical map of one request, from TCP and TLS through router, handler, service, repository, and database, and a four-question method for tracing it.
item.author: Abir Sarkar

item.title: Chapter 3: Designing Before Coding
item.description: The decisions that are expensive to reverse: Forge's requirements, invariants, lifecycle, collision policy, API contract, and failure modes, written before any Go.
item.author: Abir Sarkar

item.title: Chapter 4: The First Go Service
item.description: The smallest Forge service that honors the Chapter 3 design: Task, an in-memory store, stdlib handlers, timeouts, tests, and an honest list of what it still gets wrong.
item.author: Abir Sarkar

item.title: Chapter 5: HTTP Without the Magic
item.description: HTTP without the framework: message bytes, methods as promises, status codes, and a stricter POST /tasks that rejects the wrong type, unknown fields, and oversized bodies.
item.author: Abir Sarkar

item.title: Chapter 6: Building Handlers
item.description: A transition endpoint grows into five jobs, then is pulled apart: lifecycle rules, an atomic store update, and one error translator, so a handler only decodes, validates, calls, and responds.
item.author: Abir Sarkar

item.title: Chapter 7: Routing and Middleware
item.description: Request IDs, access logs, panic recovery, and JSON for the router's own 404 and 405. The order of the stack decides which layer can see a failure.
item.author: Abir Sarkar

item.title: Chapter 8: Validation and Error Contracts
item.description: One error shape for every failure: a stable code, a human message, field details, and a request ID. The private cause reaches the logs and never the client.
item.author: Abir Sarkar

item.title: Chapter 9: Authentication and Authorization
item.description: Users, salted bcrypt passwords, opaque session tokens, and task ownership. Authentication is middleware. Authorization is asked only once the resource is known.
item.author: Abir Sarkar

item.title: Chapter 10: API Design That Survives Change
item.description: Versioning, cursor pagination, and idempotency keys so a retry does not duplicate an effect. Part II ends with the contract a client developer would actually read.
item.author: Abir Sarkar
